title: Learning Is a Purchase. Adoption Is a Practice.
author: Rich Carr
summary: Rich Carr argues that buying or attending learning is not the same as adopting it, and that the gap explains why so much training never shows up in behavior. He cites a meta-analysis in which strong changes in intention produced about half as much behavior change, MOOC completion rates near 3 percent, and habit research showing automaticity taking anywhere from 18 to 254 days. A field experiment with high school math students shows the AI twist: an off-the-shelf chat tool boosted practice scores but hurt exam scores, while a hint-giving tutor did not, so the difference was who did the thinking. His remedy is to build adoption reps into the learning event, which he illustrates with his firm's Challenge Wheel framework and a retail onboarding case where the rehearsal group sold more than double the control. The test he offers any course is: where are the reps?
points: Wanting to use what you learned is worth about half of what it feels like, because intention only partly converts into behavior.
Habit formation depends on repetition in a consistent context, and the time to automaticity varied from 18 to 254 days in the study cited.
The AI tutoring experiment shows that identical technology can either replace or support thinking, and exam results reveal which one happened.
Moving rehearsal into the learning session, rather than assigning it as homework, is presented as the design fix for the forgetting curve.
quotes: Learning is a purchase. Adoption is a practice. They happen in different places, at different times, and only one of them is for sale.
A meta-analysis of 47 experiments found that when an intervention produced a strong change in intention, behavior moved about half as far.
The strongest factor was not insight or motivation. It was repetition in a consistent context.
Predictable lowers the threat of trying something new. Consistent makes the practice worth repeating. Kind makes the first clumsy attempt survivable.

In a field experiment with nearly a thousand high school math students, one group practiced with an off-the-shelf AI chat. During practice, they outperformed the control group by 48%. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% worse than students who never had it.
Opposite outcomes using the same machine. The difference was who did the thinking.
The old failure was learning something and never using it. The new failure is using something and never learning it.
Your brain keeps what it had to earn, and if your brain earns it, then it was your idea. You own it.
